pronunciation.approximation: Say "ahriman" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Ahriman".

kin.label: Old Avestan
kin.form: aŋrō mainiiuš, 'the evil spirit' — a common-noun phrase in the Gāthās (Yasna 30.3), not yet a fixed personal name

kin.label: Younger Avestan
kin.form: Aŋra Mainyu, the adversary proper; his creatures are the daēvas, the 'demons'

kin.label: Middle Persian
kin.form: Ahrimān, the Sasanian form from which English 'Ahriman' directly descends

pronunciation.note: Ahriman is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the form preserves nothing distinctive against ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter; it is the anglicized Middle Persian name of the Younger Avestan Aŋra Mainyu. The Gāthās know the concept (aŋrō mainiiuš, 'the evil spirit') before they know the name.

domains.title: Ahriman
domains.subtitle: Evil
domains.lead: Ahriman is the Evil Spirit of Zoroastrianism — Avestan Aŋra Mainyu, 'destructive mind' — the adversary of the wise lord Ohrmazd. He is not a rival god but the Lie made willful: choice turned against creation. The tradition is emphatic that he creates nothing, can only corrupt, and is destined to lose.

cards.name: The Twin at Dawn
cards.desc: Yasna 30's two spirits, Better and Bad, choose creation and not-being at the world's first dawn — evil begins as a choice, not a birth.

cards.name: The Lie (Druj)
cards.desc: His essence is the Lie — Avestan druj — deception and disorder that rot good choice; the daēvas are his servants.

cards.name: Counter-Creation
cards.desc: Against Ohrmazd's sky, waters, plants, cattle, and man he fashioned opposites: winter, drought, poison, wolves, and death (Bundahišn).

cards.name: The Powerless End
cards.desc: At the Renovation he is bound and defeated, his weapons melted away — eschatology grants evil no Ragnarǫk, only erasure.

symbols.name: The dragon Aži Dahāka
symbols.meaning: The three-mouthed, three-headed, six-eyed dragon he loosed against creation (Yasna 9.8; Yašt 9) — winter and lie made monster

symbols.name: Druj, the Lie
symbols.meaning: Deception as his true weapon — the dark counterpart of Aša, the order and truth that hold the good creation together

symbols.name: The north
symbols.meaning: The direction of his assault on the sky: he broke in from the north, the realm of cold and darkness (Bundahišn)

symbols.name: Winter and drought
symbols.meaning: His counter-creations against sky and water — the killing seasons raised against Ohrmazd's order

symbols.name: Wolves and xrafstars
symbols.meaning: The noxious creatures of his making — predators and vermin set against cattle, the good man's wealth

mythology.lead: Ahriman's mythology is the drama of Zoroastrian dualism: a spirit of destruction who chooses evil at creation's dawn, assaults the sky, counterfeits every good thing, and is finally bound. The fullest account is the Sasanian Bundahišn; the oldest, the Gāthās of Zarathustra.

myths.title: The Two Spirits at the First Dawn
myths.text: The oldest stratum of Zoroastrian scripture is not a battle story but a choice. In Yasna 30.3–5 Zarathustra hymns 'the two spirits in the beginning, the twins renowned as the Better and the Bad in thought, word, and deed... when the two spirits met, they created life and not-life, and settled that at the last the worst existence would be for the followers of the Lie, but the Best Mind for the followers of Truth.' The Bad Spirit — aŋrō mainiiuš — 'chose not-being' in the deed he performed. Later tradition hardened the twinhood into two eternities, but the Gāthās themselves insist on what scandalized later theologians: evil is primordial as a choice, not as a substance. The myth means that good and evil are first of all directions of the will, and every human soul stands where the two spirits once stood.

myths.title: The Assault on the Sky
myths.text: The Sasanian Greater Bundahišn (ch. 1) narrates the attack. Ahriman, in his darkness below, glimpses Ohrmazd's luminous creation and rises, envious, to destroy it. Ohrmazd — knowing the end belongs to him — offers peace: let the two realms keep to themselves for 9,000 years. Ahriman refuses; but at the first recitation of the Ahuna Vairya prayer he is thrown into stupor for three thousand years, from which the demoness Jahi the Whore wakes him with a shout. He smashes through the sky — egg-like boundary of the ordered world — from the north, and his demons pour in after him. Only then does Ohrmazd set creation in motion against him. The myth means that evil's first act is always an invasion of someone else's order: the Lie owns nothing it does not break into.

myths.title: Counter-Creation
myths.text: Ahriman's characteristic act in the Bundahišn is not creation but counterfeiting. Against Ohrmazd's sky he set the demon of winter; against water, drought and salt; against the earth, the burrowing demons; against plants, poison and the hundredfold diseases; against the sacred cattle, wolves and hunger; against man, the lie, lust, and untimely death. The text counts the diseases he fashioned at 99,999. Nothing in his inventory is original — everything is a wound answering a good thing, exactly as later doctrine says: he could not make a world of his own, and so made war on the one he found. The myth gives Zoroastrianism its sharpest answer to the problem of evil: the Devil has no substance of his own, only a talent for damage — and what can only destroy is already defeated in principle.

myths.title: The Temptation of Zarathustra
myths.text: In Vendidad 19 the adversary comes in person against the prophet. Aŋra Mainyu, with the assembled daēvas, appears to Zarathustra in the wilderness and offers sovereignty — 'we will make you ruler of the nations' — if he will abandon the praise of the Good Spirit. Zarathustra refuses, and the chapter ends with the Lie fleeing back into hellish darkness, beaten in a contest of questions that unmasks each demon's weakness. The scene is the tradition's own counterpart to the desert temptations known from later scripture, and it fixes Ahriman's method: he never merely attacks — he offers, appealing to ambition and despair, and he loses whenever a will refuses him. The myth means his power has exactly the reach of human consent; where no one listens, the Evil Spirit is already in chains.

myths.title: The Renovation
myths.text: The end of the Bundahišn grants the adversary no pyrrhic apocalypse and no equal victory. In the last three millennia the world-born saviors — the Saošyants — lead the final assault; the dead rise and pass through the ordeal of molten metal, which scalds the wicked and is warm as milk to the just; and Ahriman and the demons are thrown back, bound, and deprived of power. Some late texts go further and have him and Ohrmazd dine together on the haoma, the lie expunged. The final state is not a truce but the frashō.kereti, the making-wonderful: evil removed from creation as completely as salt from water. Against the Norse Ragnarǫk, where the old gods die in the fire, the Iranian end refuses the romance of mutual destruction. The myth means that good is not one side of a balance but the whole scale — and evil an error being corrected.

lore.syncretism: Medieval Zoroastrianism itself generated the most famous heresy about him: Zurvanism, attested in the Denkard's refutations and in Syriac and Armenian reports, made Ohrmazd and Ahriman twin sons of Zurvan, Infinite Time — evil suddenly genealogical rather than chosen, precisely the move orthodox theology refused. Outside Iran, Plutarch (De Iside et Osiride 46–47) reports the Magi and their good and evil daimones, naming the evil one Arimanius; the name turns up again in a Greek magical papyrus (PGM IV), invoked there by sorcery. Manichaeism took the figure into Middle Persian as hrywm'n, a hostile prince of darkness in the Turfan texts, and through late-antique Christian polemic his outline fed the developing theology of Satan — the 'devil as cosmic adversary' of the West owes much of its shape to the Persian-period encounter. The Achaemenid inscriptions are strikingly silent: Darius knows Auramazda and the Lie (drauga), but never the Evil Spirit by name.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ahriman never had a cult — no sane theology worships the Lie — yet his legacy is immense. In New Persian ahriman became an ordinary word for devil, and in Zoroastrian liturgy his name is ritually cursed to this day. The intellectual legacy is larger: the mature Western Devil, the 'prince of darkness' of Second Temple and early Christian writing, took much of its profile from the Persian-period encounter with Zoroastrian dualism — cosmic adversary, tempter, lord of a demonic host, destined loser. In modernity, Anquetil du Perron's 1771 translation of the Avesta reintroduced Ahriman to Europe, where he became a fixture of Romantic orientalism and eventually of scholarship — Boyce's Zoroastrians made the religion legible to a general readership. He endures in games and fantasy as the stock arch-fiend, rarely credited. The name thus tracks a long migration: from Gāthāic abstraction to Sasanian adversary to the modern world's default image of absolute evil.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Ahriman is the rarest thing in mythology: a god of evil whom his own tradition insists is not a god. The Gāthās will not let him be a second creator or an equal power; they make him a choice — the will that looked on truth and chose otherwise. What later centuries built into a towering demon-king began as something more unsettling: the recognition that evil needs no substance, only a decision, and that the decision is available to everyone, always.

This is why Zoroastrian eschatology is so strange to readers raised on Norse or Christian endings. There is no last battle whose outcome is uncertain, no twilight in which evil wins the field. Ahriman's defeat is announced at his first appearance; his entire mythology is a working-out of a foregone conclusion — which means the drama was never really about him. It is about us, standing where he stood, asked the question he was asked, and answering.
lore.archaeology: There is deliberately no archaeology of Ahriman: a cult of evil would have been unthinkable, and none existed. The material record is the scripture itself — the Avesta survives in manuscripts of a Sasanian archetype, the oldest substantial copy being the British Library's 'Avesta of 1323 CE'. The closest contemporary witness is linguistic rather than iconic: the Old Persian inscriptions of Darius I at Behistun and Persepolis name drauga, 'the Lie', as the cosmic enemy the king's order fights — Ahriman's essence without his name, some three centuries after Zarathustra. Sasanian iconography avoids his image entirely, and no sanctuary, altar, or votive has ever been identified with him. Evil's archaeological footprint is precisely an absence: the one god-shaped hole in Iran's religious landscape.
